newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 23.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 23.

text.p: Prime Minister Jim Bolger was to meet Conservation Minister Nick Smith on Monday about his request for Conservation Department chief executive Bill Mansfield's resignation, Maruia Society president Guy Salmon said. A spokeswoman for Bolger said there would be no comment about whether there would be a meeting or about the "speculation" about Smith's request. It was reported on Sunday that Smith had asked Mansfield to resign, as Smith believed Mansfield must share some of the responsibility for the Cave Creek disaster. However, under the State Sector Act, ministers do not hire ot fire government department heads.
Salmon, a friend of Smith, was alone on Sunday in his support for Smith's call for Mansfield to resign. Other groups condemned Smith as being ignorant and acting unlawfully. Page 1.

Wanganui police must take a strong line with Maoris protesting about land grievances, NZ First MP Rana Waitai says. Tempers flared in Wanganui a week ago when protestors, led by Maori activist Ken Mair, pelted a tourist houseboat on Whanganui River with rocks. Maoris took action after a tourist operator had, they said, neglected to get iwi permission to go up the river. Waitai, the former Gisborne police commander, said that
the area would succumb to lawlessness if police were lenient on protestors. Page 2.

Many conservation groups are upset about the low ranking of Conservation Minister Nick Smith, at 23rd out of 26 and outside the cabinet. But the organisations are at odds over the qualifications of Smith himself, some seeing him as capable but hamstrung, others that his record on conservation issues is not good. Forest and Bird conservation director Kevin Smith criticised Smith's sustainability in his new role. It was hard to believe that Smith would be able to resist pressures from more senior ministers who saw conservation as nothing more than an impediment to economic development, Forest and Bird's Smith said.

The sale of Hikurango forest to Malaysian interests was not against NZ First policy because it was a private sale and the forest is not a strategic asset, a spokesman for NZ First leader Winston Peters said on Sunday. Fletcher Challenge Forests sold the 24,800 hectare forest near Gisborne to Malaysian forestry company Glenealy Plantations on Friday.

Tower Corporation is moving from a passive to an active position on demutualisation. Chairman Colin Beyer said the former Government Life was the last of the main superannuation and insurance mutual societies in Australia and New Zealand to deal with demutualisation. Beyer said any decision to demutualise was ultimately in the hands of policyholders. "It would be of great benefit to them. We've seen some other examples of this recently of course." The process of demutualisation would take about two and a half years. Beyer said it would be better to go slowly than to rush it "in the way that some of the power companies have done".

Lloyds of London was expecting to issue writs against New Zealand Names with outstanding debts early nexy year, a company spokeswoman said. "We do think some will go out to people in New Zealand sometime in the new year," the spokeswoman said. She would not say how many writs would be issued in New Zealand, but confirmed they were dependent on the outcome of proceedings before British courts. The action is part of a huge debt-recovery campaign by the 308-year-old insurance company against members who have refused to accept its settlement package to help the company fix past financial problems.
